name: iron

attributes.attribute: a folkloric motif, the substance fairy folk dreaded more than any other
its word comes from the Celtic iarn, adopted into Latin and spread through Europe
a child replaced by fairies, prevented when a nail is hidden in the birth bed

sources: Dorson, Richard M., ed. Peasant Customs and Savage Myths: Selections from the British Folklorists. Vol. 2. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1968, 25.
hEochaidh, Séan. Fairy Legends of Donegal. Translated by Máire MacNeill. Dublin: Comhairle Bhéaloideas Éireann, 1977. Page 167.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Iron is a folkloric motif. Fairy folk dreaded iron more than any other substance. People carried nails in a pocket when they passed a fairy rath. They put nails in the bottom of milk pails to keep fairies from stealing milk. A mother hid a nail in her bed during birth. This protected the child from becoming a changeling. Iron crosses repelled fairies. Iron scissors worked if held open to form a cross. These traditions appear across the Celtic lands. Their source is unclear. The Celts were among the earliest Europeans to work iron. Their metalwork was renowned. It brought wealth through trade with their neighbors. The very word iron comes from a Celtic word, iarn. Latin adopted it and spread it through Europe. Some scholars say the fairies were originally the gods of pre-Celtic peoples. Their fear of iron may reflect a historical conflict.

okr.objective: Document iron as a Celtic folkloric motif.
key_results: Record the folk practices using iron to repel fairies.
Note the Celtic origin of the word iron from iarn.
Offer the scholarly view connecting fairy fear of iron to a historical conflict.
